title: Pentecostalism worldwide
hookLine: from a plain mission on Azusa Street to Pentecostal churches across Africa, Asia and Latin America

lines: SIDE BY SIDE IN ONE ROOM.
cards: No stained glass. No steeple. No pews.
On Azusa Street in Los Angeles, a plain wooden building, once used as a stable and a storeroom, has sawdust on the floor and planks laid across barrels for benches.
At the front stands a preacher named William Seymour, the son of formerly enslaved parents, with a pair of wooden crates for a pulpit.

In the room, Black and white and Latino worshipers, washerwomen and businessmen, side by side, in a city and a country that kept them apart. People pray out loud, weep, sing, and some speak in tongues.

teach.b: Pentecostalism takes its name from Pentecost, the day in Acts when the Holy Spirit comes on Jesus's followers in Jerusalem.
In the King James Bible: "And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance."

Then Peter stands up and quotes the prophet Joel: "I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy." Pentecostals read that as a promise for now, not only for then.
Speaking in tongues, prophecy, prayer for healing: the gifts of the Spirit, they say, are for ordinary believers today. And it showed in who led.

teach.h: WOMEN PREACHED, THE COLOR LINE BLURRED.
teach.b: At Azusa Street, women preached, and Black and white Christians laid hands on one another, which shocked plenty of observers. One early participant wrote, in effect, that the color line had been washed away.
It didn't stay washed; Pentecostal churches later split along racial lines too, and that's part of the story. Some historians say the movement didn't spread from one center like spokes from a hub.
They point to revivals with similar marks around the same era in India, Korea, Chile and parts of Africa, many led by local preachers rather than visiting missionaries.
Today Pentecostal and charismatic churches are found from Lagos to Seoul to São Paulo, and charismatic renewal has reached Catholic and older Protestant churches too. Christians differ here.
Pentecostals say the gifts continue. Some other Christians hold that certain gifts, like tongues, belonged to the apostles' time. Both read the same chapter of Acts.

how: Pentecostal worship is often loud and expressive, with long sung praise, raised hands, spontaneous prayer, prayer for healing, and speaking in tongues. Charismatic groups in Catholic and other churches pray in similar ways within their own traditions.

games.q: you're leading the meeting on Azusa Street. who gets to pray and preach at the front?
o: whoever the Spirit moves: women and men, Black and white.
only the preacher at the crates.
games.why: women preached and Black and white believers prayed over each other. Pentecostals pointed to Joel: "your sons and your daughters shall prophesy."

practice: Bring to mind a Pentecostal or charismatic church you've passed: a rented room above a shop, a big hall by the highway, a congregation meeting in a school gym on Sundays.
Picture the people walking in, the music starting, someone raising their hands, and let yourself be curious rather than wary. If you pray, pray for that congregation.

wordCard.voice: Pentecostalism worldwide. A movement that reads Pentecost as a promise for today, with gifts of the Spirit for ordinary believers, now found across Africa, Asia and Latin America.
